clue.text: Wild West character, diffident about dicky bow

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so one word goes round the other
dicky is slang for unsound or shaky, so the word beside it is knocked out of its usual order

explanation.surface: A rough frontier figure who feels shy about wearing a bow tie.
explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled BOW sits inside COY: CO-WBO-Y gives COWBOY.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy is the stock cattle-herding figure of American frontier stories set in the Wild West.

clue.text: Actors run out with president

parts.note: the cast is the set of actors in a show
cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out

explanation.surface: Actors flee the stage alongside a head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: RO is how a scorecard records a batter run out.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidel and Raúl Castro each served as president of Cuba.

clue.text: Be the dominant one in stormy weather over devastated US resort

indicators.note: stormy means turbulent, so the word beside it is tossed into a new order
devastated means wrecked, so these words are torn apart and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A storm sweeps over an American holiday town and wrecks it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'over' puts the first part above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear the trousers is an idiom for being the one in charge in a household or relationship.

clue.text: Lyric poem about a concert hall

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: A poem written about a concert venue.
explanation.definitionFit: An odeon was a building in ancient Greece for musical performances; the name later passed to cinemas.

clue.text: None left? Very well

definitions.meaning: playful meaning: if none is on the left, every one is on the right side
second meaning: an expression of agreement, okay

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical reading: nothing left means everything is right. The second is the everyday phrase of assent.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying it in agreement is the same assent as 'very well', a grudging okay to a request.

clue.text: Weapon made from pine, hollow mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: to pine is to long for something

explanation.surface: A bow carved from hollowed-out pine wood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' looks like the timber; it is the verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: The longbow was the tall bow of medieval English archers, a ranged weapon.

clue.text: Coach, amongst others, shows self-discipline

indicators.note: amongst means in the middle of, so one word sits inside the other

explanation.surface: A sports coach mixing with others displays self-control.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint is holding oneself back, the same quality as self-discipline.

clue.text: Good former worker has drink after getting retirement present

parts.note: a hand is a worker, as on a farm

explanation.surface: A good ex-employee has a drink after receiving a leaving gift.
explanation.definitionFit: A golden handshake is a large payment given to someone on retiring or leaving a job.

clue.text: Good order — tons ordered inside by head of state

indicators.note: ordered means arranged, so the letters are set out in a new sequence

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for tons
taken as written, part of the fodder

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Neat order: tons of stuff arranged indoors by a head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' looks like a container signal but is plain anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidiness is the state of being neat and well arranged, in good order.

clue.text: I'm deep in trouble, in check

indicators.note: something in trouble is in disarray, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone admits being in serious difficulty, perhaps in check at chess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In check' sounds like chess; check is simply the verb to hold back.
explanation.definitionFit: To impede is to hinder or obstruct, which is what checking progress means.

clue.text: Distinguished politician, say, on South Island

parts.note: the Isle of Man, between Britain and Ireland

explanation.surface: A notable politician reports from some southern island.
explanation.definitionFit: A statesman is a respected, experienced political leader, a cut above an ordinary politician.

clue.text: Youth attached to Salvation Army serves up a cold dish

parts.note: a lad is a young man

explanation.surface: A young volunteer with the Salvation Army hands out cold food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attached to' puts the youth after the Army's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Salad is a dish of raw or cold vegetables, typically served chilled.

clue.text: Body of aides in suite

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the attendants accompanying an important person
second meaning: a suite is also a group of attendants

explanation.walkthrough: 'Suite' suggests a hotel room for the aides, but it is the older sense of a train of followers.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of attendants following a dignitary, also called an entourage or suite.

clue.text: Shoot British, then drive on

parts.note: to urge is to drive or push forward

explanation.surface: An order to fire at the British and then keep driving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' reads as firing a gun; it is the verb for a plant sprouting.
explanation.definitionFit: To burgeon is to sprout or put out new growth, as a plant shoots.

clue.text: Be afraid of heavy objects catching the boxers

definitions.note: the answer has no article; 'the' is part of the wordplay too

indicators.note: catching means grabbing hold of, so one word closes round another

parts.note: to fear is to be afraid

explanation.surface: Someone nervous of heavy weights while sparring with boxers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' does double duty in the surface: it introduces the boxers but is also caught by the fear. 'Heavy' points away from the light class in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Featherweights are boxers in a light weight division, so the class names the fighters.

clue.text: Exile in entrance

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to deport convicts overseas, as Britain did to Australia
second meaning: to enrapture, carry away with emotion (entrance as a verb)

explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' reads as a doorway noun; it is the verb to enchant.
explanation.definitionFit: Transport historically meant shipping convicts abroad, and also means to fill someone with delight.

clue.text: Vehicle used for racing, extremely swift? A crock, anyhow

indicators.note: anyhow means in a careless, haphazard way, so the letters fall in any order
extremely points to the extremes of the word, its outermost letters

explanation.surface: Is a battered old wreck really a fast racing car?
explanation.walkthrough: A crock is an old, broken-down car.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock car is a reinforced ordinary saloon car raced on oval tracks, often with collisions.

clue.text: One who needs backers for a book?

definitions.text: One who needs backers for a book?

parts.words: One who needs backers for a book?
parts.note: surface reading: an author or publisher seeking financial backers for a book
setter's reading: backers are punters placing bets, and a book is the record of wagers a bookmaker keeps

explanation.walkthrough: In racing, 'backers' bet on horses and a 'book' is the bookmaker's ledger of bets, not a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Turf accountant is a jokey British formal term for a bookmaker, who takes bets on horse races.

clue.text: Quality of weapon's bore?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: standard or worth of a person or thing
second meaning: the internal diameter of a gun barrel

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase about a gun; split it, and 'of' is just a joint.
explanation.definitionFit: Calibre measures a gun barrel's internal diameter and, figuratively, the merit or standard of something.

clue.text: Arduous at college? Hard? Hardly

parts.note: in British usage you are up at university during term
ill means badly or scarcely, as in 'can ill afford'

explanation.surface: A student wonders whether university is hard, and decides it hardly is.
explanation.definitionFit: An uphill task is one that is difficult and tiring, like climbing a slope.

clue.text: Ruler in Lombardy, nastiest

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the answer lies inside the following words

explanation.surface: The cruellest ruler in the Italian region of Lombardy.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynast is a hereditary ruler, a member of a ruling dynasty.

clue.text: Uncle, so upset with lawyer

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: An uncle is distressed and has hired a lawyer.
explanation.definitionFit: Counsel is the term for a barrister or lawyer acting in a case.

clue.text: Gossip from judge, for example

explanation.surface: Tittle-tattle passed on by a judge, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearsay is information heard from others rather than known directly, much like gossip or rumour.

clue.text: A Caledonian in English town

parts.note: Caledonia is the old name for Scotland

explanation.surface: A Scotsman living in an English town.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a Berkshire town known for its royal racecourse.

clue.text: Set of beliefs held by sacred Order

indicators.note: held by means contained in, so the answer sits inside the following words

explanation.surface: A creed kept by a holy religious order.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a creed, a statement of the beliefs someone holds.

clue.text: Warm hat Bacall knitted girl

indicators.note: knitting works yarn into a new form, so these letters are worked into a different arrangement

parts.note: a girl's name, as in Ava Gardner

explanation.surface: Lauren Bacall knitting a woolly hat for a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A balaclava is a close-fitting woollen hood covering the head and neck, worn for warmth.

clue.text: Left the ground, test ground, with badges

indicators.note: ground here is the past of grind, so the word is crushed and remade

parts.note: rose means went up into the air

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: players leave the Test ground wearing badges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' appears twice: first as the earth, then as the past of grind, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosettes are ribbon badges awarded as prizes or worn to show support.

clue.text: Making every allowance for amateur bowled in international match

indicators.note: in places one item inside another, so the cricket letter goes into the match

parts.note: a Test is an international cricket or rugby match

explanation.surface: An amateur cricketer dismissed during a Test match.
explanation.walkthrough: A comes first, then TEST with B inside it after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: At best qualifies a claim to its most favourable reading, as when making every allowance.
